items.learnMore:
Capacity vs. capability

Capacity is about room; capability is about ability. The engineer in the Scenario has three committed deadlines, which is a capacity fact, not a doubt about skill.

Common mistake

Treating every decline as an admission of inability.

The company's strategy

items.prompt: What does the manager know that the engineer may not?

a promise to work evenings

items.prompt: A manager asks for a fourth project. Which reply best uses trade-off framing?
choices: I can start Monday if Q3 reporting moves back a sprint
Honestly, I am simply too busy to take on anything further this quarter
I will work out how to fit it in around my existing projects somehow

items.reference:
Who holds which information
speaker knows: what is already committed
requester knows: how urgent the new item is
the trade-off offer brings both together
Why: the decision belongs where both pieces of information meet.
items.learnMore:
Trade-off framing

State what is committed, then offer the choice: take the new work and move something, or decline and keep the plan. The requester decides with the real cost visible.

Common mistake

Treating the offer as a polite refusal instead of a real choice.
items.reflection: Think of a request you accepted without naming its cost. Who ended up paying it?

The manager decides with authority and the engineer stops guessing priorities
The engineer is never asked for extra work again after using it
The manager no longer needs to understand the details of any project
items.explanation: Each side gets what it lacked: authority to choose, and clarity about what matters more.

Credible capacity signals

Reaching for 'I'm busy' because it is shorter to say.

items.prompt: What flaw do the three hidden-cost moves share?

items.prompt: An engineer quietly takes a fourth project and ships the first three a week late. What is the central failure?
choices: No one with authority ever chose to delay the first three
The engineer refused to work any extra evenings at all
The fourth project was not important to the business
The first three projects had deadlines that were too early
items.explanation: The slip happened by default, never put in front of the person who owned it.
items.reference:
Who decides what slips
silent absorption: nobody decides
flat refusal: speaker, unexplained
deciding alone: speaker, without consent
trade-off offer: the requester, with facts
Why: the cost is real either way; only one path lets the right person choose it.
items.learnMore:
When the trade-off stays hidden

Silent absorption, an unexplained refusal and a unilateral choice all keep the person with authority from seeing the choice. The cost moves somewhere nobody picked.

Common mistake

Believing silent absorption is the safe option.
items.reflection: Where have you absorbed extra work quietly? Who would have chosen differently if they had known?
